Chapter 2 — Why AI Matters for Business Leaders: The MBA Imperative
LM Thapar School of Management, Thapar Institute of Engineering & Technology, Derabassi Campus
Prepared by Dr. Amit Kumar Bhardwaj
Session 2 | Module 1: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
"AI literacy is no longer a differentiator on a résumé. It is fast becoming the baseline assumption behind every strategy, operations, and general-management role a business school prepares its graduates for." — Chapter opening reflection
2.1 Opening Vignette: The Interview Question Nobody Used to Ask
Five years ago, a campus recruiter interviewing for a strategy-consulting role might ask a candidate to walk through a market-sizing exercise or a case on pricing. Today, the same interview increasingly includes a different kind of question: "Which AI tools have you used to support an analysis, and how did you validate the output?" The shift is not cosmetic. It reflects a structural change in what employers believe a business graduate must be able to do on day one — and it is the reason this course exists as a required, not elective, part of the curriculum.
This chapter makes the business case for AI literacy before this book turns, in the chapters that follow, to the technical vocabulary and history that make that literacy possible. It answers a question every student implicitly asks in the first week of any required course: why does this matter, and why now?
2.2 AI in the Business School Curriculum
AI's presence in management education has moved from experimental to structural in a remarkably short window. Business schools across geographies — including several of the most selective institutions globally — now weave AI into everything from tutoring and skills-building to core strategy courses and career guidance, rather than confining it to a single specialised elective.

2.3 The Employer Demand Signal
The clearest evidence that AI literacy is now a baseline hiring criterion, not a bonus skill, comes from employer-side data rather than from business schools themselves.
74% of employers specifically screen for AI/ML proficiency in MBA graduates — a rise that has moved AI literacy from roughly the 21st most sought-after competency to the 4th (e-GMAT).
66% of organisational leaders report they will not hire a candidate who lacks demonstrable AI literacy (Microsoft CDN).
Recruiters increasingly expect AI fluency by default, particularly for roles in strategy and operations, where AI-assisted analysis has become a normal part of the workflow rather than a novelty (AI Literacy Institute).
For a general-management graduate, the practical implication is that AI literacy now functions less like a specialised technical skill and more like spreadsheet literacy did a generation ago: a baseline competency assumed by default, whose absence is noticed far more than its presence.

2.5 The Readiness Gap
LM Thapar School of Management, Thapar Institute of Engineering & Technology, Derabassi Campus
Prepared by Dr. Amit Kumar Bhardwaj
Student behaviour has already moved ahead of formal curricula. Surveys consistently show students using AI tools weekly, and often daily, across a wide range of academic tasks — essay writing, brainstorming, data analysis, and simulation among them. Business schools have responded by layering structured, hands-on experiences on top of this organic usage: AI-enabled class projects, dedicated workshops, and competitive formats such as datathons run in partnership with organisations including Bloomberg and Amazon, designed to convert informal tool familiarity into disciplined, evaluable skill.
High usage does not equal high competence, and this is the gap this course is built to close. Even where adoption is widespread, formal training remains inconsistent — one recent UK study found only around 36% of students received institutional support for AI skill-building. The gap is not primarily technical; it concerns strategy, ethics integration, and the equipping needed for deep, responsible use rather than superficial tool familiarity. A student who has used a chatbot to draft an essay has not thereby learned to evaluate an AI-generated business recommendation for bias, groundedness, or fitness for a board-level decision. Closing that specific gap — between casual usage and disciplined managerial judgement — is the throughline of this entire textbook.
2.6 A Ladder of AI Proficiency: Where This Course Sits
AI education is often organised into three broad proficiency tiers, moving from general literacy through hands-on model-building to advanced engineering and research. Understanding this ladder helps calibrate expectations for BA5306: this course is designed to take students confidently through the Basic tier and into the early stages of the Intermediate tier — building working fluency and applied judgement, not developer-level engineering skill, which the syllabus's Module 6 transition into "Responsible AI and AI Specialisations" exists to serve for students who want to go further.

fabricated competitor revenue figure at face value simply because it was delivered fluently and confidently —
precisely the failure mode covered in this course's later discussion of generative AI governance (Chapter 23).

Every field's founding definitions reveal what its founders believed mattered most — and AI's definitions have shifted meaningfully as the technology itself has matured. LM Thapar School of Management, Thapar Institute of Engineering & Technology, Derabassi Campus
Prepared by Dr. Amit Kumar Bhardwaj

Many disappointing AI deployments trace back to a system being asked to reason or decide when it was, in reality, only ever built to perceive or classify.

2. Using the three-level proficiency ladder, honestly place your own current AI skill level. What would move you one level up in the next six months?
3. Recall a tool or product you have heard described as "AI-powered." Using the five core capabilities, which one is it most plausibly demonstrating — and which is it probably not?

Chapter 3 — The Evolution of AI: From Turing to Generative Intelligence
LM Thapar School of Management, Thapar Institute of Engineering & Technology, Derabassi Campus
Prepared by Dr. Amit Kumar Bhardwaj
Session 3 | Module 1: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
"AI did not arrive suddenly in 2022. It arrived in cycles of hype and disappointment stretching back seventy years — and the manager who understands that rhythm is far better equipped to judge today's claims than one who assumes the current wave is the first." — Chapter opening reflection
3.1 Why History Is a Managerial Tool, Not a Trivia Exercise
It is tempting to treat the history of AI as background colour — interesting, but not directly useful to a manager deciding whether to fund a generative-AI pilot next quarter. This chapter argues the opposite. AI has already lived through two full boom-and-bust cycles, each driven by the same underlying pattern: capability improves, expectations outrun capability, funding collapses when the gap becomes visible, and the field re-emerges only once a genuine technical unlock closes that gap. Recognising this pattern is one of the most transferable skills this course can offer a general manager evaluating any new wave of AI hype
including the current one.

The formal discipline of AI traces to a specific, datable set of events rather than a gradual drift. In 1950, Alan Turing proposed what became known as the Turing Test in his paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," asking the deceptively simple question, "Can machines think?" In 1956, the term "Artificial Intelligence" itself was coined at the Dartmouth Conference — widely regarded as the field's official founding moment. By 1959, Arthur Samuel had built one of the first machine-learning programs, a checkers-playing system capable of improving its own performance through experience.
3.3.1 The Turing Test (1950)
Proposed by Alan Turing, the test asks whether a machine can exhibit behaviour indistinguishable from a human's: a human evaluator holds a text conversation with both a machine and another human, and if the evaluator cannot reliably tell which is which, the machine is said to exhibit intelligent behaviour. Its significance lies in introducing the very concept of machine intelligence as something testable, and it laid the theoretical groundwork that inspired decades of AI research. Its acknowledged limitation, evident from the very first chatbots built to chase it, is equally important: a machine only needs to imitate human conversation convincingly — it does not need to understand what it is saying.
3.3.2 The Logic Theorist (1956)
Developed by Allen Newell and Herbert A. Simon at the RAND Corporation, the Logic Theorist proved 38 mathematical theorems from Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica — in some cases finding more elegant proofs than the human mathematicians who originated them. It is widely considered the first true AI program, and its presentation at the Dartmouth Summer Research Project is treated as the moment the field of AI was formally born. Together, the Turing Test defined what it would mean for a machine to be considered intelligent, while the Logic Theorist demonstrated that symbolic machine reasoning was achievable in practice.

AI's dramatic acceleration after 2012 was not the result of a single breakthrough insight but of three separate technological trends converging at the same moment — each pioneered by identifiable people and institutions, and each necessary but not sufficient on its own.
The synergy is the important managerial lesson here, not any one component in isolation: AlexNet's landmark 2012 victory in the ImageNet competition — a top-5 error rate of just 15.3%, roughly 10.8 percentage points better than the runner-up's 26.2% — depended simultaneously on deep convolutional networks (the algorithm), large labelled datasets (the fuel), and GPU acceleration (the engine). (The "top- 5" qualifier matters: it means the correct label appeared among the model's five most likely predictions, a standard and appropriately generous measure for a 1,000-category task — not a claim that AlexNet was correct 85% of the time on its single best guess.) Remove any one of the three enablers and the breakthrough does not happen on the same timeline. The same logic applies to evaluating a firm's own AI readiness today: data, compute, and algorithmic capability must be assessed together, not as independent checkboxes.

AI's dramatic acceleration after 2012 was not the result of a single breakthrough insight but of three separate technological trends converging at the same moment — each pioneered by identifiable people and institutions, and each necessary but not sufficient on its own.

The synergy is the important managerial lesson here, not any one component in isolation: AlexNet's landmark 2012 victory in the ImageNet competition — a top-5 error rate of just 15.3%, roughly 10.8 percentage points better than the runner-up's 26.2% — depended simultaneously on deep convolutional networks (the algorithm), large labelled datasets (the fuel), and GPU acceleration (the engine). (The "top- 5" qualifier matters: it means the correct label appeared among the model's five most likely predictions, a standard and appropriately generous measure for a 1,000-category task — not a claim that AlexNet was correct 85% of the time on its single best guess.) Remove any one of the three enablers and the breakthrough does not happen on the same timeline. The same logic applies to evaluating a firm's own AI readiness today: data, compute, and algorithmic capability must be assessed together, not as independent checkboxes.

3.9 Era 5 — Generative AI and Modern Milestones (2018–Present)
Transformer-based architectures (including BERT and GPT) gave rise to today's foundation-model era: GPT-3, DALL·E, and ChatGPT emerged between 2020 and 2023, followed by an explosion of multimodal models, enterprise-scale LLM deployment, and accelerating AI regulation. Three milestone systems in particular trace AI's expansion from narrow, single-domain problem-solving to general-purpose language capability, and are worth studying individually.
3.9.1 IBM Watson — Question Answering at Scale (2011)
Built to compete on the American quiz show Jeopardy!, Watson defeated the show's two most celebrated human champions in 2011. Its DeepQA architecture combined natural language processing, information retrieval, machine learning, and statistical reasoning to parse complex language — including puns — and infer answers from vast unstructured data. Watson's significance for business lay less in the game-show win itself than in what followed: its subsequent application to healthcare (cancer diagnosis support), finance (risk management), and legal services demonstrated, for the first time at this scale, that AI could move credibly from a lab demonstration to real-world enterprise problem-solving.
3.9.2 AlphaGo — Strategic Intuition (2016)
Created by DeepMind, AlphaGo defeated world Go champion Lee Sedol in 2016 by combining deep neural networks with reinforcement learning — studying millions of expert games and then playing against itself millions more times, guided by Monte Carlo Tree Search for efficient decision-making. Its descendant, AlphaZero, went on to master chess and shogi with no human game data at all, and its underlying self- play approach directly influenced later scientific-discovery tools such as AlphaFold.

3.9.3 GPTs — Language Understanding and Generation (2018–Present)
OpenAI's Generative Pretrained Transformers evolved rapidly: GPT-1 (2018) was a small-scale proof of concept; GPT-2 (2019) was the first widely capable language model, initially withheld over safety concerns; GPT-3 (2020), with 175 billion parameters, became the most powerful large language model of its time; and GPT-4 (2023) added multimodal capability, handling images alongside text with markedly improved reasoning. GPTs ushered in the generative AI era proper, powering tools such as ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, DALL·E, and Whisper, and reaching a scale of adoption — millions of users worldwide, including SMEs and non-technical sectors previously locked out of AI capability — that sparked global conversations about AI ethics, hallucination risk, workforce disruption, and regulation.

Reflection Questions
1. Pick one system from the chatbot lineage (Section 3.4) and identify a modern business tool that shares its core limitation. What would it take to fix that limitation today?
2. Compare the first AI Winter (1970s) to any current AI-adjacent hype you have observed. What early warning signs from the 1970s, if any, are visible today?
3. Of the three AI-comeback enablers — Big Data, GPUs, Deep Learning — which is your own organisation strongest in, and which is the binding constraint on its AI ambitions?

Executive Takeaways
AI's seventy-year history organises cleanly into five eras — Thinking About Intelligence, Rule-Based
Conversation, Knowledge and Learning, Deep Learning, and Generative AI — each defined by a single
question the field was trying to answer.
The chatbot lineage from ELIZA (1966) through Cleverbot (2011) previews nearly every failure mode still
relevant to evaluating a conversational AI vendor today, especially the gap between convincing surface
behaviour and genuine understanding.
Both historical AI Winters followed the same pattern — limited expectations and inadequate compute
produced disappointing results, which triggered funding collapse — and that pattern remains the single
best diagnostic for stress-testing today's generative-AI hype.
The post-2012 AI comeback rested on three converging enablers — Big Data, GPUs, and Deep Learning
algorithms — pioneered by named individuals and institutions; readiness today should still be assessed
against all three, not any one in isolation.
Watson, AlphaGo, and GPTs mark AI's progression from narrow question-answering, to intuition-driven
strategic mastery, to general-purpose language generation — three distinct and increasingly general
capability leaps, each with direct, current business analogues.
India's AI policy landscape — the IndiaAI Mission, Bhashini, and related initiatives — is directly relevant
to this course's BSIS regional-impact mandate and gives students a domestic case for AI's economic and
governance stakes.
